speaker: Rafael Broshi
en: And what happened was, is that the product was great. I mean, everyone said it was great. It sounded genius. The only problem was, and that's a big problem. There was no product market fit. It means that there was no real pain that we were solving by offering this kind of product. If you were in a coffee shop and you heard someone talking about an idea, OK, that they're actually executing on. OK, a startup three months ahead of you, that they're actually building something and when you hear it, you understand that's exactly the product you want to build. Would you be happy about it saying, oh my God, I can learn some stuff, or will you be completely bummed about it that someone beat you to it? He said, of course I'll be bummed. I said, so why don't you want to tell about your idea, right? Put it everywhere. No one's going to want to do it. That's where I figured out if we get to an enterprise kind of POC and we figure out a way to be a front runner in the race with less than a week of preparation. That means that we have a good product that already fits those kinds of clients.
zh: 后来发生的情况是，产品很棒。我的意思是，大家都说它很棒。听起来像天才之作。唯一的问题是，而这可是个大问题。没有产品市场契合度。这意味着我们提供这种产品并没有解决真实的痛点。如果你在一家咖啡馆里，听到有人在谈论一个点子，好吧，他们正在实际执行的点子。好吧，一家比你领先三个月的创业公司，他们确实在造某个东西，而当你听到时，你明白那正是你想做的产品。你会为此感到高兴吗，说，天哪，我可以学到一些东西，还是会为别人抢在你前面而彻底沮丧？他说，我当然会沮丧。我说，那你为什么不想讲出你的点子呢，对吧？到处去讲。没人会想去做的。就是这样我才想明白，如果我们能在一家企业级的 POC 中，用不到一周的准备时间就能在这场竞赛中成为领跑者。那就意味着我们有一个已经契合这类客户的优质产品。

speaker: Rafael Broshi
en: There was this one large contract. I think it was the first seven figure deal that we closed in a land and not a land and expand motion. That was a large insurance carrier where, I remember we got into a POC, not in an ordinary fashion. We got through the back door at the middle of a POC that has been already running, which is pretty good in terms of shortening the sale cycle but it's usually very bad and puts you at a disadvantage because you don't really know where you're working on. We don't know the environment, you don't really know the people that well, you haven't had time to plan and figure out what exactly you had to do. And I think what was really the light bulb moment was after we brought in the first version. The POC had three versions that we had to provide to the client in the AI customer experience space and the idea was that they did not want us to continue to iterate every day on making the product better, but just put up three versions. One every couple of days where they would run thousands of tests. It was a very, very detailed kind of POC where they had people involved throughout the process. It was tech valuation, it was product valuation, it was team valuation and validation. It's a four year contract, a large one with a large enterprise. So the whole deal, and I think that after we brought in the first version, where they told us, look, you were not in the initial phases of the POC, but what we expect is 1, 2, 3 and we had essentially the weekend. We got that on Thursday afternoon and on Monday, we had to figure out and give the second version. So we worked our asses off. It was a team of like six, seven people on that POC. We slept two nights at the office to get that second version up and running. But once the second version hit, suddenly the entire conversation kind of changed from us being the underdog and giving us a chance just because they wanted another vendor in the POC, and they said, "Why not? We already set up the infrastructure too". Oh my God, those guys can actually win and I think that's where I figured out if we get to an enterprise kind of POC and we figure out a way to be a front runner in the race with less than a week of preparation. That means that we have a good product that already fits those kind of clients. Going forward a few weeks, we actually won the POC, got the contract and we're working with this client, and we're now in production, and it's a massive contract. But I think that kind of second iteration, where we saw we're up there in the race, that's where when I figured out we had something that people actually want, and we don't have to completely rebuild something. Because I think that's the part where a lot of people are kind of confusing between product market fit of a product you currently have, or that you have a great team that can execute very fast and be agile. And you build something else that might fit whatever the POC wants.
zh: 有一份很大的合同。我记得那是我们以纯新签而非新签加扩张模式拿下的第一笔七位数订单。那是一家大型保险公司，我记得我们进入了一个 POC，但不是以寻常的方式。我们是从后门进入一个已经在进行中的 POC 的中间阶段，这在缩短销售周期方面相当有利，但通常也非常糟糕，会让你处于劣势，因为你并不真正清楚自己在什么环境中工作。我们不了解环境，你对那里的人也不够熟悉，你没有时间计划和弄清楚你到底该做什么。我认为真正的灵光一现时刻是在我们提交第一版之后。POC 要求我们向客户提供三个版本，那是在 AI 客户体验领域，他们的想法是不要我们每天持续迭代改进产品，而是一共提交三个版本。每两天一版，他们会运行数千个测试。那是一个非常、非常细致的 POC，他们全程都有人参与。有技术评估，有产品评估，有团队评估和验证。那是一份四年的合同，与大企业签的大单子。所以整个交易，我认为在我们提交第一版之后，他们告诉我们，听着，你们没有参与 POC 的最初阶段，但我们期望的是 1、2、3，而我们实际上只有周末。我们是周四下午收到通知的，到周一，我们就得弄出并交付第二版。所以我们拼了命地干。那个 POC 上有大概六七个人的团队。为了把第二版跑起来，我们在办公室睡了两晚。但一旦第二版交付，突然之间整个对话的基调变了，从我们是处于劣势、他们只是因为想让 POC 里多一家供应商才给我们机会，变成，天哪，这些人真的能赢。我想就是在那时我明白了，如果我们能在一家企业级的 POC 中，用不到一周的准备时间就成为这场竞赛的领跑者。那就意味着我们有一个已经契合这类客户的优质产品。往后推几周，我们真的赢了那个 POC，拿到了合同，我们现在还在和这个客户合作，我们已经进入生产环境，这是一笔巨大的合同。但我认为正是第二轮迭代，让我们看到自己在这场竞赛中位居前列，那一刻我才明白我们拥有的东西是人们真正想要的，我们不必完全推倒重建。因为我认为很多人容易混淆的一点是：是你当前已有的产品达到了产品市场契合度，还是你拥有一支执行极快、足够敏捷的优秀团队。而你另造出的某个东西可能恰好契合 POC 想要的。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: How big was this contract?
zh: 这份合同有多大？

speaker: Rafael Broshi
en: That was around a million dollars, a bit more per year.

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: And tell me a little bit about, you know, you came in late, then you were the front runner. Maybe give me context on what it is the product does and why you think you went from last entrant to front runner through that second version.
zh: 那跟我讲讲，你知道的，你们是后进场的，然后成了领跑者。也许给我一些背景，这个产品到底是做什么的，以及你为什么认为自己能从最后入场者通过第二版变成领跑者。

speaker: Rafael Broshi
en: Sure, so our platform is a platform to build and deploy AI agents, in the customer experience space and back office space. Essentially, we take processes in large regulated organizations such as carriers, banks, and asset managers, and we help them automate those processes. In this case, that was a project in the customer experience space, where that carrier wanted to completely revamp their customer operations. That means that people that want policy servicing, that have questions about their policies, want to do some changes, get general information. That they'll be able to get information 24/7 accurately through AI, and because it is an insurance carrier, and highly regulated industry, there is no room for hallucinations. The quality has to be extremely, extremely high and there's a lot of things related to compliance and audit trail that you need to adhere to. So the POC was essentially take a very large corpus of public information, tens of thousands of pages from the website and other kind of sources. Take a mock API with personal information about a set of example customers, not real customers. Plus do a few, I'd say simple processes such as add a new driver to your insurance policy. So take all of those and then provide a chat interface for their team to try out your AI bot, AI agent, as if they were clients. And then, they have a set of thousands of different tests that I wanted to make sure that the more information you digest and the more information what we're seeing with those kind of AI tools. The more information and the more guidelines, and the more processes that you're trying to cover, the lower the quality of the responses. And that's what they wanted to check that there is no degradation because they already knew that the problem is not really figuring out what works in a POC if the POC is very, very short. Is that those kind of products don't scale in production and then things starts to break, and it's extremely, extremely hard to fix those mistakes. Because at some point, if you use a very simple architecture of one prompt, then the kind of context size causes the AI agent to hallucinate, to not be as accurate and it's very, very hard to fix. So that's what they wanted to figure out.
zh: 当然，我们的平台是一个用于构建和部署 AI 智能体的平台，面向客户体验和后台运营领域。本质上，我们把大型受监管组织（如保险公司、银行和资产管理公司）的流程拿来，帮它们实现自动化。在这个案例中，那是客户体验领域的一个项目，那家保险公司想彻底翻新他们的客户运营。也就是说，那些想要保单服务、对保单有疑问、想做些变更、想获取一般信息的人。他们将能够通过 AI 全天候准确地获取信息，而因为这是一家保险公司，属于高度受监管的行业，没有出现幻觉的空间。质量必须极其、极其高，而且有很多合规和审计追踪方面的事情需要遵守。所以那个 POC 本质上是：取一个非常庞大的公开信息语料库，来自网站和其他来源的数万页内容。取一个包含一组示例客户（不是真实客户）个人信息的模拟 API。再加上做几个，可以说是简单的流程，比如往你的保单里加一名新司机。把所有这些拿过来，然后为他们的团队提供一个聊天界面，让他们像客户一样试用你的 AI 机器人、AI 智能体。然后，他们有数千个不同的测试，他们想确认：你消化的信息越多，我们在这类 AI 工具上看到的情况就是，信息和指南越多，你想覆盖的流程越多，回答的质量就越低。而那正是他们想检查的：不存在质量退化，因为他们已经知道，问题并不在于在 POC 里弄清楚什么有效——如果 POC 非常、非常短的话。问题在于这类产品在生产环境中无法规模化，然后事情开始出问题，而修复那些错误极其、极其困难。因为在某个节点上，如果你用的是一个非常简单的单提示词架构，那么上下文规模就会导致 AI 智能体产生幻觉、不够准确，而且非常、非常难修。所以那就是他们想弄清楚的。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: And what do you think you did? Maybe it's just technical, but is there a simple way of understanding what you did relative to the others? I mean, again, I'm asking you because in the respect of a founder selling enterprise, going through POCs, the odds that you're going up against others, very high, right? It's not like SMB sales, where it's just like, you go on a demo, they're like, oh, this is cool, I'll buy it. So you always got to think about where am I actually, you think your product is great or are you actually relative to the others. I don't know if you can share maybe some more details around that because that was the key piece, was that not just did you do it. You did it better than the others and then therefore you became kind of the number one choice.
zh: 那你觉得你们做对了什么？也许纯粹是技术层面的，但有没有一种简单的方式来理解你们相对于其他家做了什么？我是说，再问一次，我问你这个，是因为站在一个卖企业级产品、要过一道道 POC 的创始人的角度，你要和其他人对阵的几率非常高，对吧？这不像 SMB 销售，那就像是，你去做个演示，他们说，哦，这挺酷，我买了。所以你总得想想自己实际处在什么位置，你觉得你的产品很棒，还是你实际上相对其他家如何。我不知道你能不能再多分享一些细节，因为那才是关键：不只是你们做到了。而是你们比别人做得更好，因此你们成了那个第一选择。

speaker: Rafael Broshi
en: So I think it all starts with the kind of point of view that we had when we started. So we actually started the company five years ago in the insurance space as a managing general agent. So we actually sold an insurance policy ourselves and started building a product internally to help us service our own policyholders. And then time went on, we closed the insurance product because we saw that the software we built internally to help us service our policyholder is more relevant. And because we came from a regulated space, from insurance, and we built the product to service ourselves. It was always more than a GPT wrapper that helps you answer FAQ. Because we were the one at stake here. It's not like you're selling a product and then you say, hey, good luck. I gave you the tool. You're going to be fine with it or not. It's that we were in charge of our own destiny. If someone would have sued us because our AI made a mistake, I'm the one who was supposed to handle that kind of lawsuit. So I think we build the product from an architectural standpoint a lot different, where when complexity increases it's not that we increase the prompt size. We increase the number of components of AI, components of LLMs that we use. So essentially when complexity increases, we increase compute, and we built things very, very differently in order to adhere to very accurate and very high standards in, production and complex environments. That's the main difference, very technical in that regard, but I think that's what won us the POC.
zh: 我想一切都始于我们创立之初的那个视角。所以我们实际上五年前是从保险领域起步的，当时是一家管理总代理。所以我们实际上自己卖过保单，并开始在内部构建一个产品来帮我们服务自己的保单持有人。后来时间推移，我们关掉了保险产品，因为我们看到我们在内部构建的、用来服务保单持有人的软件更有价值。而且因为我们来自受监管领域、来自保险业，而且我们是为服务自己而构建的产品。所以它从来都不仅仅是一个帮你回答 FAQ 的 GPT 套壳。因为押上身家的就是我们自己。这不一样——不是你卖出一个产品然后说，嘿，祝你好运。工具给你了，你用得顺不顺利与我无关。而是我们掌控着自己的命运。如果有人因为我们的 AI 犯了错而起诉我们，负责应对那场官司的人是我。所以我认为我们从架构层面构建产品的方式就有很大不同：当复杂度上升时，我们不是去增大提示词的规模。我们是增加 AI 组件、增加我们所用 LLM 组件的数量。所以本质上，当复杂度上升时，我们增加算力，而且我们把东西造得非常、非常不一样，以便在生产环境和复杂环境中达到非常精确、非常高的标准。那是主要区别，在这方面非常技术化，但我认为那就是让我们赢下 POC 的原因。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: And maybe, last question before we kind of go to the story. I've met many startups who close one enterprise customer and it's easy to think when you close one enterprise customer, whether it's 100K or 500K. That, well, if you closed one, you've done the hard part. You just got to do this ten times, twenty, fifty times, whatever. You're on the road already, which is not the same again. With SMB, it's like, I've got ten customers. Doesn't really mean you're going to get to a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand, which is what you probably need. But with enterprise there's some of that, you know, logically, if you could get one, why can't you get ten? But oftentimes it just doesn't happen. You get the one and you kind of get stuck there. In your case, you're describing this POC, this moment as product market fit. Which entails that it wasn't just the fact that you got this contract, but it was going to lead to a lot more from a lot of others. Do you have a sense of what it was about this that gave you that feeling? That gave you a feeling that not only did we win $1 million contract, which is great, but that this signifies that we're going to win a lot other million dollar contracts?
zh: 那么也许，在我们进入故事之前最后一个问题。我见过很多初创公司拿下一个企业客户，而当你拿下一个企业客户时，很容易去想，无论是 10 万还是 50 万的。想着，好吧，你拿下一个了，最难的部分已经完成了。你只要把这个重复十次、二十次、五十次，随便多少次。你已经在路上了，这又不完全一样。SMB 的话，就像，我有十个客户了。这并不真正意味着你能到一百个、一千个、十万个，而那可能是你需要的。但企业客户方面确实有几分这个道理，你知道的，从逻辑上讲，如果你能拿下一个，为什么不能拿下十个？但很多时候它就是不发生。你拿下那一个，然后就卡在那儿了。在你的案例里，你把这个 POC、这个时刻描述为产品市场契合度。这意味着不只是你拿到了这份合同这个事实，而是它将带来来自其他许多客户的更多合同。你有没有一种感觉，知道是什么给了你那种感觉？那种感觉是：我们不只是赢下了一份 100 万美元的合同，这很棒，而且这标志着我们将赢下很多其他百万美元的合同？

speaker: Rafael Broshi
en: It's a great question and it really depends on why you won. A lot of companies that get stuck with one or two enterprise clients. It's because they're becoming sort of like their personal dev shop and essentially think about it. Every enterprise that decides to work with a small startup, whether it's ten people, twenty, fifty, a hundred, and there are five thousand, ten thousand people company. Why would they want to work with you, right? They want the speed and they want customization, right? They know that everything they're going to ask, you're going to execute and you're going to execute fast for them. So if you won the POC versus a large, let's say vendor. Because you customized everything about your system to fit what the client wanted, well, I'm not saying it's bad. Sometimes it's needed, but that should be kind of a yellow light in your head.
zh: 这是个好问题，而这真的取决于你为什么赢。很多卡在一两个企业客户上的公司。是因为它们变得有点像那些客户的私人开发外包团队，本质上你想一想。每一家决定和一个小初创公司合作的企业，不管是十人、二十人、五十人、一百人的，而对面是五千人、一万人的公司。他们为什么想和你合作，对吧？他们要的是速度，他们要的是定制化，对吧？他们知道他们提的每一个要求，你都会执行，而且会为他们快速执行。所以如果你赢下 POC 是因为，比方说对阵一家大型供应商。因为你把系统的方方面面都定制化去迎合客户想要的，嗯，我不是说这不好。有时候这是需要的，但这在你的脑子里应该算是一盏黄灯。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: That's a risk, yeah. That makes sense.
zh: 那是一种风险，对。有道理。

speaker: Rafael Broshi
en: That's a risk but if at the end of the day, you're saying, hey, I did not have to change anything. I just had to prepare the demo in the right way, or I just had to tweak, or I just had to do two integrations to meet their requirements. Then that's totally different and if at the end of the day what you hear from them are very, I'd say generic things that they were looking for, so this was not a POC of hey, you need to create an entire pipeline that connects to our policy admin system and then to our own internal CRM, and then to this, and then to that, something that is very, very unique. But it's we want something that responds fast, that takes a huge corpus of data, that has an audit trail, that is deployed on prem, which is something we do that others don't. If you hear those kind of generic things that people always tell you when you're starting to sell to enterprise, that it's not only about your features, it's the entire kind of holistic picture of how you deploy your services. So I think that's a pretty good green flag as to maybe you have something, although working with enterprise is a lot more than the product. The fact that you need to commit to SLAs, you need a team. This is not a small customer where you can say, oh yeah, we have a bug. We'll talk in two days, right? You're getting a phone call within four minutes from their SOC team. You have to deliver, otherwise there are penalties and it's not a joke, right? Winning an enterprise contract is the easiest part of working with an enterprise.
zh: 那是一种风险，但如果到头来你说的是，嘿，我什么都没改。我只是用正确的方式准备了演示，或者我只是微调了一下，或者我只是做了两个集成来满足他们的要求。那就完全不同了，而如果到头来你从他们那里听到的是一些非常，可以说是通用化的诉求，所以这不是那种 POC——嘿，你需要创建一条完整的管道，连到我们的保单管理系统，再连到我们自己的内部 CRM，再连到这个，再连到那个，某种非常、非常独特的东西。而是我们要一个响应快的、能消化海量数据语料的、有审计追踪的、部署在本地的产品，而部署在本地是我们做而别人不做的事。如果你听到的是这类通用化的东西，人们刚开始向企业销售时总会跟你讲的那些，那就不只是关于你的功能，而是关于你如何部署服务的整体图景。所以我认为这是一个相当好的绿灯，说明你也许有点东西，尽管和企业合作远不止产品本身。你需要承诺 SLA，你需要一个团队。这不是那种你可以说，哦对，我们有个 bug。我们两天后再谈的小客户，对吧？你会在四分钟内接到他们 SOC 团队的电话。你必须交付，否则就有罚则，这不是开玩笑，对吧？赢下企业合同是和企业合作这件事里最容易的部分。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: So let's go back now in the story. You mentioned you started this five years ago, so about 2021. Give me just a little bit of your background and then, maybe the origin story about what it was that you started and why you started it.
zh: 那我们现在回到故事里。你提到你是五年前开始的，所以大约是 2021 年。先简单讲讲你的背景，然后，也许讲讲起源故事：你最初做的是什么，以及你为什么做它。

speaker: Rafael Broshi
en: Sure, so I spent ten years in the Air Force. I quit and then I used to work for a startup. After that, I worked for a hedge fund and after two years I decided enough is enough, and I wanted to start something. And a good friend of mine that at the time worked as a product manager. We decided to start something, bought another good friend who was a team lead and back then in 2021, and I said we started in the insurance space. There was a huge hype around crypto, around creator economy. So we created a new insurance product for digital assets. That means that if you lose your digital asset due to an account takeover due to a hack, you're getting insured for it and it was a real insurance product that we launched in the US. So that's how we started, then we started growing, ChatGPT came out, that was November 2022. We started playing around and said, hey, we're starting to scale in the US. We have many policyholders. We don't want to scale headcount. We were VC backed, but we did not have a lot of money back then. So we had to build a product that will help us service our clients while we grow and that's how the internal product started. And that's where we are today.
zh: 当然，我在空军待了十年。我退了役，然后曾为一家初创公司工作。在那之后，我在一家对冲基金工作，两年后我决定受够了，我想做点什么。我一个好朋友当时做产品经理。我们决定一起做点什么，又拉上另一个当时做团队负责人的好朋友，那时候是 2021 年，我说了我们是从保险领域起步的。当时围绕加密货币、围绕创作者经济有巨大的炒作。所以我们为数字资产创造了一款新的保险产品。也就是说，如果你的数字资产因为账户被接管、因为被黑客攻击而损失，你会为此获得赔付，而且这是一款真实推出的保险产品，我们在美国上线了它。我们就是这么开始的，然后我们开始增长，ChatGPT 问世了，那是 2022 年 11 月。我们开始摆弄它并说，嘿，我们正开始在美国扩张。我们有很多保单持有人。我们不想扩张人力。我们是有 VC 投资的，但那时候我们没什么钱。所以我们得造一个能帮我们在增长的同时服务客户的产品，这就是那个内部产品的起点。也就是我们今天所在的地方。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: You started in the crypto space and then you ended up now in the AI space. One way which came and went, most startups that start in one wave. Especially the first wave, doesn't really work. It's hard to ride the next one, right? So let's just go deeper on that. Tell me a little bit more about the product you build and how that, up and down went, and then we can move through that story.
zh: 你从加密领域起步，然后你现在进入了 AI 领域。有一个浪潮来了又走了，大多数从一个浪潮起步的初创公司。尤其是第一波，其实并不成。很难骑上下一波，对吧？那我们就深入聊聊这个。多讲讲你造的那个产品，以及它的起起落落，然后我们可以顺着故事往下走。

speaker: Rafael Broshi
en: Sure, so essentially we built an insurance product, we started selling it in the US. Launched in forty seven states, in the admitted market. The insurance market has two separate markets, the admitted is the more regulated one. We had to be backed by a real insurance carrier, in this case they were out of Hartford, Connecticut. They endorsed us to be able to launch in forty seven states. So, the US is not one market. It's fifty different markets, which makes it extremely difficult to scale and what happened was that the product was great. I mean, everyone said it was great. It sounded genius. The only problem was, and that's a big problem. There was no product market fit. It means that there was no real pain that we were solving by offering this kind of product.
zh: 当然，本质上我们造了一款保险产品，我们开始在美国销售。在四十七个州、在准入市场上线。保险市场有两个分开的市场，准入市场是监管更严的那个。我们必须有一家真正的保险公司做背书，在这个案例里他们来自康涅狄格州哈特福德。他们背书我们，让我们能在四十七个州上线。所以，美国不是一个市场。它是五十个不同的市场，这使得扩张极其困难，然后发生的情况是，产品很棒。我的意思是，大家都说它很棒。听起来像天才之作。唯一的问题是，而这可是个大问题。没有产品市场契合度。这意味着我们提供这种产品并没有解决真实的痛点。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: This is insurance for crypto assets?
zh: 这是加密资产的保险？

speaker: Rafael Broshi
en: That was insurance for social media accounts and crypto assets for digital assets in general, and what you learn from that experience is that it's very, very, very hard. And I don't think it is a startup's job to change a market or create awareness, OK. Yes, you have to ride waves as a startup. If you're lucky, you're going to start and the wave is going to grow with you. But you need to look at a market that is opening. It's like an earthquake when you see the earth shatters and you start seeing a shift, and you start seeing a huge gap. OK, that's exactly what happens now or when we started in the AI for customer experience space, right? So something happened, new technology, ChatGPT came out, a consumer app based on that technology. That made everyone open their eyes and say, wait, I can now offer better support. I can now cut costs. I can do things that everyone tried to do for fifteen years with NLP, et cetera, but didn't work. And that, also meant that every company that has tried to do that up until this point and have poured millions of dollars or hundreds of millions of dollars. Now at that moment, there was an even playing field. Everyone that put money on that was thrown away. Obviously their distribution remains the platform, like Intercom or Zendesk. But in terms of technology, you had the exact same shot of succeeding as Salesforce or Zendesk, et cetera. So I think those kinds of shifts in the market, unlike where we were in insurance, where we had to educate the market. There were a lot of tailwinds. It's a very kind of traditional market where you don't see a lot of new insurance products going to market. The newest insurance product that went to market is probably Cyber and it went to market in like 1997 and only caught up in 2015. So I don't think that's where you should fight. So a lot of people think that starting a startup or building a new product means we're innovating on every kind of layer, right? We're innovating on technology, we're innovating on an idea and what they expect is that when they tell the idea to someone, someone would say, oh my God, this thing is genius. But in most cases, from what I've seen from friends who succeeded or you can see about it online, that's the exact opposite reaction. What you're usually getting, what we got when we were in the insurance business is, wow, that's genius. Everything was genius other than the fact that not a lot of people wanted to buy it. Right now or when we started AI for customer support, the main feedback we got is, isn't everyone doing it? And, that's a bummer but you shouldn't care, right? Because innovating usually means innovating in one place. You're innovating in distribution, you're innovating on service, you're innovating on technology, you're innovating on simplicity and product features, on time to value. But not a lot of companies are able to build a completely new space. By the way, OpenAI with ChatGPT, yes, they built something completely new but even they started in 2015, and they created something that changed the world. But this is not the ordinary story of a startup.
zh: 那是针对社交媒体账户和加密资产的保险，广义上的数字资产，而你从那段经历里学到的是，这非常、非常、非常难。而且我不认为改变一个市场或创造认知是创业公司该干的事，好吧。是的，作为创业公司你得骑浪潮。如果你运气好，你起步的时候浪潮会和你一起长大。但你需要看向一个正在打开的市场。就像地震一样，你看到大地裂开，开始看到位移，开始看到一个巨大的裂缝。好吧，这正是现在发生的事，或者说我们当初进入 AI 客户体验领域时发生的事，对吧？某件事发生了，新技术来了，ChatGPT 问世了，一个基于那项技术的消费级应用。这让每个人都睁开了眼睛，说，等等，我现在可以提供更好的支持了。我现在可以削减成本了。我可以做到那些大家用 NLP 等等尝试了十五年都没做到的事。而那也意味着，到那时为止尝试过这件事、并砸进数百万美元或数亿美元的每一家公司。在那一刻，赛场被拉平了。所有在那上面投过钱的人都出局了。显然它们的分发渠道还在，平台还在，比如 Intercom 或 Zendesk。但在技术层面，你成功的几率和 Salesforce 或 Zendesk 等等完全一样。所以我认为市场中的这类转变，不同于我们当时所在的保险业——在那里我们不得不教育市场。这里有大量的顺风。那是一个非常传统的市场，你看不到多少新保险产品进入市场。最新进入市场的保险产品大概是网络保险，它大约在 1997 年进入市场，到 2015 年才真正起量。所以我认为那不是你该战斗的地方。很多人觉得创办一家初创公司或造一个新产品意味着我们在每一个层面上都在创新，对吧？我们在技术上创新，我们在想法上创新，而他们期待的是，当他们把想法讲给别人听时，别人会说，天哪，这东西是天才之作。但在大多数情况下，据我从成功了的朋友那里看到的，或者你在网上能看到的，你得到的恰恰是相反的反应。你通常会得到的，我们当年做保险生意时得到的，是，哇，太天才了。一切都很天才，除了没有多少人想买它这个事实。而现在，或者说我们开始做 AI 客服时，我们得到的主要反馈是，不是所有人都在做这个吗？而这确实令人沮丧，但你不该在意，对吧？因为创新通常意味着在某个地方创新。你在分发上创新，你在服务上创新，你在技术上创新，你在简洁性和产品功能上创新，在价值实现时间上创新。但没有几家公司能够凭空造出一个全新的领域。顺便说一句，OpenAI 和 ChatGPT，是的，他们造出了全新的东西，但即便是他们也是 2015 年起步的，而且他们创造出了改变世界的东西。但这不是一个创业公司的寻常剧本。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: It's so true and I find it especially the case if I talk to somebody. Let's say not in the startup world or not a successful founder and like a late person, whatever. And I'm telling them about companies I work with, the ones that are probably doing the best get the least attention. He's like, well, this doesn't sound that cool. The ones that are having the most trouble because they went for something so crazy. Those are the ones that are like, wow, that's the game changer one. But to make that into reality, yeah, you've got the Elon Musk's of the world or whatever, and I think maybe if you're a hyper successful founder who can attract insane amounts of capital. You know, at the get go, who can have incredible kind of relationships at the biggest levels and that's what it takes to move a market, by the way. And even then, not to say that your odds of success are high, it's just maybe then you have a fighting chance. But if you're a first time founder or even a repeat founder that's not Elon Musk level repeat founder, it's true. These are most of the things that work. Decagon is a great example. I mean, Decagon is like a $5 billion business today doing AI for customer experience. If I were to tell somebody that didn't know that story, it's like, how? What do you mean? Isn't that a solved problem? A lot of these things you think are solved problems are not and, you have to go and talk to, like in your case, the person that actually is doing this initiative at an insurance company that can tell you, actually, there's budget for this right now. We're trying to solve this right now, and we haven't solved it yet. And then you're in the right place, right time.
zh: 太对了，而且我发现尤其当你和某个人聊的时候更是如此。比方说不在创业圈里的人，或者不是一个成功的创始人，或者一个后知后觉的人，随便什么人。我跟他们讲我合作的公司，那些做得最好的得到的关注最少。他说，嗯，这听起来没那么酷。而那些麻烦最多的公司，因为它们冲了某个太疯狂的东西。那些反而是让人说，哇，那才是改变游戏规则的。但要把它变成现实，是的，你得是埃隆·马斯克那样的人物之类的，而且我觉得也许如果你是一个极其成功的创始人，能从一开始就吸引天量资本。你知道的，谁能在最高层级拥有惊人的关系，顺便说一句，那才是撬动一个市场所需要的。而且即便那样，也不是说你的成功几率就高，只是那样你也许才有一战之力。但如果你是第一次创业的创始人，甚至是一个连续创业者但不是马斯克级别的连续创业者，这是真的。这些才是大多数能成的路子。Decagon 就是一个绝佳例子。我是说，Decagon 今天就像一家 50 亿美元估值的公司，做 AI 客户体验。如果我去讲给一个不了解那段故事的人听，对方会说，怎么会？什么意思？这不已经是被解决的问题了吗？很多你以为已经被解决的问题并没有，而且，你得去和——就像在你的案例里——保险公司里真正负责这个行动的人聊，那个人能告诉你，实际上，现在有这笔预算。我们现在正在试图解决这个问题，而我们还没解决。然后你就处在了正确的地方、正确的时间。

speaker: Rafael Broshi
en: Yeah, exactly. I think what you said last is spot on. You want to build something where there's a budget for it right now, or you're very confident that there's going to be a budget for it in the next six to twelve months. The thing is, those kind of tech waves. If they haven't started yet, they might start tomorrow or in five years. It's still very, very close. But if it starts in three years, you're not gonna be there, you're gonna start building too early. Even if you don't run out of money by the time the wave  starts. Someone that started building two years after you will have better technology and less tech debt, right? So building something for a wave that's going to come has a high reward, but it's incredibly difficult, and usually what happens is you think you're late but you're incredibly early, right? When we started I said, wow, we're late, we're incredibly late, but no, we were early. So same here, right? People think about, you know, AI for carriers, right, for insurance carriers, and you see all those McKinsey reports and seventy percent of carriers said they're using AI. Yes, they have 45,000 people, they're using AI, they might have replaced one person with the kind of efficiency. It's like a lot of carriers haven't even moved to cloud yet.
zh: 对，没错。我觉得你最后说的那点一针见血。你要造一个现在就有预算的东西，或者你非常有信心在未来六到十二个月内会有预算的东西。问题是，这类技术浪潮。如果它们还没开始，它们可能明天开始，也可能五年后开始。那仍然非常、非常近。但如果它三年后才开始，你就不会在场了，你会开始得太早。即便你在浪潮开始之前没烧完钱。比你晚两年开始的人会有更好的技术和更少的技术债，对吧？所以为一个将要到来的浪潮造东西回报很高，但难到难以置信，而通常发生的情况是，你觉得自己晚了，但其实你早得不可思议，对吧？我们开始的时候我说，哇，我们晚了，我们晚得离谱，但不，我们其实很早。这里也一样，对吧？人们谈到 AI 用于保险公司，对吧，保险行业的公司，你会看到所有那些麦肯锡报告，70% 的保险公司说他们在用 AI。是的，他们有 45000 名员工，他们在用 AI，他们也许用那种效率替换了一个人。很多保险公司甚至还没上云呢。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Yeah, that's what I was gonna say. I mean, that's the one that I always go back to. Cloud's been around for a long time. People are still moving to cloud just to give you a sense of how long it takes.
zh: 对，那正是我要说的。我是说，那是我总会回头引用的例子。云已经存在很长时间了。人们到现在还在迁向云，只为让你感受一下这需要多长时间。

speaker: Rafael Broshi
en: Yeah, we just spoke to a large carrier that sends status updates of a life claim by mail, physical mail, every three weeks. It happens a lot in the US. So there's going to be a huge transformation now in AI. It's not going to take a year. It's not going to take two years. Enterprise takes time. It's going to take five, ten, fifteen years. The only difference is that unlike cloud, what I think we're going to see is that companies in commoditized industries, such as insurance or banking, where the products are pretty similar, will not have the opportunity to wait for three years and say, hey, let's wait for those things to work and then we'll start. Because companies that are not going to jump in right now are going to be so far behind because of the kind of leverage you get with AI. It's going to be incredibly hard to close. OK, so that's what I think makes this wave a bit different than others.
zh: 对，我们刚和一家大型保险公司聊过，他们的寿险理赔状态更新是靠邮寄、实体邮件发送的，每三周一次。这在美国很常见。所以现在 AI 领域会有一场巨大的转型。它不会花一年。它不会花两年。企业级需要时间。它会花五年、十年、十五年。唯一的区别是，我认为与云不同的是我们将看到的：处于商品化行业（比如保险或银行）的公司，产品都大同小异，将没有机会等上三年说，嘿，我们等这些东西成熟了再开始。因为现在不立刻跳进来的公司会落后太多，因为 AI 带来的那种杠杆。差距会难以置信地难追。好吧，所以这就是我认为这波浪潮和其他浪潮有点不一样的地方。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: It's just a faster wave. Yeah.
zh: 它只是一波更快的浪潮。对。

speaker: Rafael Broshi
en: Yeah. It's a faster wave where you're seeing the kind of crazy technology that you'd imagine those kind of financial services players adopt in five or ten years. They're adopting it now, OK so e-commerce players adopted it eighteen months ago. Banks, asset managers, insurance carriers, credit unions. Now's the time they're starting to implement those solutions.
zh: 对。这是一波更快的浪潮，你会看到那些你以为这类金融服务玩家要五到十年才会采用的疯狂技术。他们现在就在采用，好吧，比如电商玩家十八个月前就采用了。银行、资产管理公司、保险公司、信用合作社。现在正是他们开始实施这些方案的时候。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: We have tens of thousands of people who have followed the show. Are you one of those people? You want to be part of the group. You want to be a part of those tens of thousands of followers. So hit the follow button. Tell me more about making that pivot. Like when was it that you decided to go for this AI for customer experience? And what was it that drove you there? Because if I'm putting myself in the founder's shoes, that's probably the biggest thing is, OK, we all know AI is a wave, but I'm right now thinking about where to kind of focus in. Where do I go? How do I catch the space that's the earthquake? How do I catch the space that's going to adopt really quickly? So how did you do it?
zh: 我们有数以万计关注这个节目的人。你是其中之一吗？你想成为这个群体的一份子。你想成为那数以万计关注者中的一员。那就点一下关注按钮。多跟我讲讲那次转型。比如你是什么时候决定做这个 AI 客户体验的？是什么驱动你走到那里？因为如果我把自己放在创始人的位置上，那可能是最大的难题：好吧，我们都知道 AI 是一波浪潮，但我现在在想该往哪个方向聚焦。我该去哪里？我怎么才能抓住那个正在发生地震的领域？我怎么才能抓住那个会非常快被采纳的领域？那你是怎么做的？

speaker: Rafael Broshi
en: Yeah, so first of all, everything looks obvious in hindsight. And we were there when it started. Nothing is obvious. And even if it's obvious, there are always risks, right? So when we decided to pivot, because we said in the insurance part, we're growing, but we're not growing fast enough. We decided to pivot. It took us months to understand what to do, even though we had that platform that helps us respond to questions of customers, real customers in a real company that does business. And even then it took us months to say what we're going to do. And just timeline wise, by the way, when is this? That was in 2023. It's like, first of all, when a wave starts, you're not sure if it's a wave or if it's just the hype cycle. NFTs. OK. Now you're going to see Twitter blowing up. You're going to see Mark Andreessen changing his profile picture and Twitter to an NFT, right? The world's going to go nuts and you're going to say, well, I don't know if that makes sense. Like I wouldn't buy the Mona Lisa as an NFT. And some people might hear this and then write emails to me of how stupid I am and how NFTs are going to change the world. Right. But it's much easier to be at this point in time with the conviction to say, I think NFTs were a fad. I could not have said that in 2021 or 2022, right? You would have been an outcast if you said it. You might not have joined, but you would have been an outcast. So when a wave starts, it's incredibly hard to understand. By the way, it's also hard right now because what's going to happen, everything in life works in cycles, right? Tech hype cycles. So now we're at a hype. What's going to happen soon is we're going to see that AI costs are through the roof. Companies aren't seeing ROI. Then a company that IPOs is going to drop by forty percent because of that. And then the hype cycle of AI will die. And obviously I do think, and everyone agrees, that it is a trend. But there's going to be a dot com time sometime in the future, right? I don't know how hard this is going to hit, but it is going to hit. So I think that's one. It's very hard to understand. But what we said is, look, do we believe AI is going to be a wave that transforms the world? Yes. If we look back thirty years in the future, will we regret not being there? We think we're at a point of the year 1998, we're going to start with AI, ninety nine percent of companies are going to go bankrupt or blow out. There's going to be a ton of competition, but will we regret not trying to compete in this way? You said yes. OK, great. We want to go there then, going through what we suffered in the insurance space where we built something very small. We said we're not going to build something small. We're going to build something that has the potential to be huge, and it is so obvious that no one's ever going to ask us why would someone need it. It's going to be the most obvious thing in the world. What's AI going to do? AI is going to replace workforce, awesome. Where are the three areas that we think today, that was three years ago, that is going to work, OK? We didn't talk about developers and everything related to coding because we're not that deep tech and it's not us. We said, OK, that's going to be in sales, marketing, customer support sales. Well, sales is really tough and I am still not a big believer of automated SDRs. Marketing, well, interesting, but it's not really our forte. Customer support. OK, we've done customer support. The ROI is very easy to explain. It's very easy to explain to any company. Hey, you have a hundred people. We can make it so you have twenty people. Great. How much money do you save? Plus you're going to offer 24/7 service, localization, better support, better QA, blah, blah, blah. OK. Very easy. You said, OK, great. AI for customer support, and that's how it started. And since then, no one ever asked me, why would someone need it? OK. It's the exact same question. Isn't it a solved problem yet? Aren't there a ton of competition? What are you doing differently? Why would someone work with you and not with Salesforce? Like those are the kinds of questions we get.
zh: 对，首先，事后一切看起来都是显而易见的。而浪潮开始的时候我们就在场。没有什么是显而易见的。即便它显而易见，也总伴随着风险，对吧？所以我们决定转型时，因为我们在保险那部分业务里说，我们在增长，但我们增长得不够快。我们决定转型。我们花了好几个月才想清楚要做什么，尽管我们已经拥有那个平台，它帮我们回答真实公司里做真实生意的真实客户的问题。即便那样，我们也花了好几个月才说要做什么。顺便按时间线说，这是什么时候？那是 2023 年。就是说，首先，当一个浪潮开始时，你不确定它是一波浪潮，还是只是炒作周期。NFT。好吧。接下来你会看到 Twitter 上炸开了锅。你会看到 Marc Andreessen 把他的 Twitter 头像换成 NFT，对吧？全世界会为之疯狂，你会说，嗯，我不知道这讲不讲得通。比如我不会把蒙娜丽莎买成 NFT。也许有些人听到这个会给我写邮件，说我多愚蠢、NFT 将如何改变世界。对。但站在现在这个时点带着确定感说，我觉得 NFT 是一阵风，要容易得多。在 2021 年或 2022 年我可说不出这话，对吧？你要是说了，你就会被排斥。你可能没有入伙，但你会被排斥。所以当一个浪潮开始时，要理解它是极难的。顺便说，现在也很难，因为接下来会发生什么，生活中一切都以周期运转，对吧？技术炒作周期。所以我们现在处于一个炒作高点。接下来很快会发生的是，我们会看到 AI 成本高得离谱。公司看不到 ROI。然后某家 IPO 的公司会因此跌掉百分之四十。然后 AI 的炒作周期会死掉。而显然我确实认为，而且所有人都同意，这是一个大趋势。但未来某个时候会有一次互联网泡沫式的时刻，对吧？我不知道这会有多狠，但它一定会来。所以我认为这是第一点：要理解它非常难。但我们当时说的是，听着，我们相信 AI 会成为改变世界的一波浪潮吗？信。如果我们回望三十年后的未来，我们会为不在场而后悔吗？我们觉得自己正处在相当于 1998 年的时点，我们要开始做 AI，百分之九十九的公司会破产或倒下。会有海量的竞争，但我们会为不以此为方向去竞争而后悔吗？你的答案是会。好吧，好。那我们就去那里，经历过我们在保险领域吃的苦——我们造了一个很小的东西。我们说我们不要造小东西。我们要造一个有潜力变得巨大的东西，而且它是如此显而易见，以至于永远没有人会问我们为什么会有人需要它。它会是世界上最显而易见的东西。AI 会做什么？AI 会替代人力，很好。那今天我们认为——那是三年前——会成立的三个领域是哪些，好吧？我们没有谈开发者和一切与写代码相关的东西，因为我们没有那么深科技，而且那不是我们。我们说，好吧，那会是在销售、营销、客户支持里。嗯，销售非常难，而且我至今仍不太信自动化 SDR。营销嘛，有意思，但不是我们真正擅长的。客户支持。好吧，我们做过客户支持。ROI 非常好解释。对任何公司都非常好解释。嘿，你有一百个人。我们可以做到让你只要二十个人。很好。你省了多少钱？而且你还会提供全天候服务、本地化、更好的支持、更好的质检，等等等等。好吧。非常简单。你说，好吧，很好。就 AI 客服了，事情就是这么开始的。而从那以后，从来没有人问过我，为什么会有人需要它？好吧。大家问的是完全一样的问题。这不还是个已被解决的问题吗？竞争者是不是一大堆？你们做的有什么不同？为什么会有人和你合作而不和 Salesforce 合作？我们收到的就是这类问题。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Yes, of course. And I'm curious, like at that time, 2023, I mean, this is still two years ago, three years ago. So there were, there probably weren't that many, like it was probably happening, but it's not like there were like AI customer support winners. There would have been like the 2.0, like the previous wave chatbot customer support winners. So you had that going for you, but did you find sometimes spaces appear way more crowded than they really are? And like, isn't everybody selling? And then you get into it and you talk to the customer and you're like, actually it's you and these two, like it's not thirty, right? What was actually your experience?
zh: 是，当然。而且我很好奇，比如在那个时候，2023 年，我是说，那也才是两三年前。所以当时，大概还没有那么多，事情大概在发生，但还不至于已经有 AI 客服的赢家。那时候有的会是 2.0，比如上一波聊天机器人客服的赢家。所以这是你的优势，但你有没有发现，有时候一些领域看起来比实际拥挤得多？比如，不是所有人都在卖吗？然后你进了场、和客户聊，你说，实际上就是你和这两家，根本不是三十家，对吧？你实际的经历是什么？

speaker: Rafael Broshi
en: Yeah. So it's pretty close to what you said when we started. We said everyone's doing it, but we haven't seen so many VC backed startups doing it because everyone thought everyone's doing it.
zh: 对。所以和我们开始时你说的很接近。我们当时说所有人都在做，但我们没看到那么多有 VC 投资的初创公司在做，因为所有人都以为所有人都在做。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Nobody's backing them.
zh: 没人投它们。

speaker: Rafael Broshi
en: And it's like, when I ask people, I want to. I'm asking them about their idea or people want to consult with me and say, well, I don't, I don't want to launch. I don't want to tell people what I'm doing and I said, look, if you were in a coffee shop and you heard someone talking about an idea, that they're actually executing on. A startup three years, three months ahead of you, that they're actually building something and when you hear it, you understand that's exactly the product you want to build. Would you be happy about it saying, oh my God, I can learn some stuff, or will you be completely bummed about it? That someone beat you to it? He said, of course, I'll be bummed. I said, so why don't you want to tell about your idea, right? Put it everywhere. No one's going to want to do it. So I think that's what happened. So what we saw were either larger companies from past generation, OK. Salesforce, or that was Zendesk and Ada, and other companies like that. That either had older chatbots going into the AI era, or we saw those kind of solopreneurs. The kind of people that did chat with PDF when ChatGPT started, and you heard stories of people making $5 million in two months with PDF. Before ChatGPT killed that and just added the option to add a PDF. So same thing, you know, you saw small companies like that building those fast chatbots, doing a quick buck. But then we said, OK, there is no way they're going to be able to compete long term with the VC backed startup. It's just not going to happen and then you saw in the same time that we did that, there were the larger companies in stealth mode in the US, right? The Sierras, the Decagons, et cetera. But that's what we saw in the beginning. What we're seeing now is the second part of what you said, the area is not that crowded. There aren't a lot of players out there that can deploy on prem with a company in a regulated space, to have the kind of capability that they would require with the same level of compliance and security. And being able to meet their SLA and data requirements. There aren't a lot, OK. We're seeing the same players over and over again. It's not seventeen players, it's not. OK, you can count them on one hand and also the horizontal players, we don't see them that often as well, right? So when you verticalize yourself, or it doesn't matter what you do, right? But when you pick a specific kind of box to play in, we feel that at this space, we don't see many. Now, if we're going to go down and we started before going to financial services. When we built the product in 2023, we started selling to e-commerce and in e-commerce. Obviously we saw more players, but smaller players as well. But again, same few names popped up and I know you have the competition is for losers by Peter Thiel, et cetera. And again, who am I to say something different? But I'll say I don't think competition is what kills startups at our stages, right? It's competition makes you do stupid things like copy other players or go toward the second different direction. Say, oh, those guys succeed there. Let's go there. Oh, they're doing this. So it must be good. But no, those guys are exactly like you. They have no idea what they're doing. Everyone in the space has no idea what they're doing at this stage. So competition makes you do stupid things, not because it forces you, but just because it's part of our nature.
zh: 就像，当我问别人，我想做。我问他们他们的点子，或者有人想找我咨询然后说，嗯，我不要，我不想发布。我不想告诉别人我在做什么，然后我说，听着，如果你在一家咖啡馆里，听到有人在谈论一个点子，他们正在实际执行的点子。一家比你领先三年、三个月的创业公司，他们确实在造某个东西，而当你听到时，你明白那正是你想做的产品。你会为此感到高兴吗，说，天哪，我可以学到一些东西，还是会彻底沮丧？为别人抢在你前面？他说，我当然会沮丧。我说，那你为什么不想讲出你的点子，对吧？到处去讲。没人会想去做的。所以我想事情就是这样。所以我们看到的无非是，来自上一代的大公司，好吧。Salesforce，或者说那是 Zendesk 和 Ada，以及类似的公司。它们要么带着老旧的聊天机器人进入 AI 时代，要么我们看到的是那种单人创业者。就是 ChatGPT 刚出时做 chat with PDF 的那类人，而且你听过那些故事，有人靠 PDF 两个月赚了 500 万美元。在 ChatGPT 杀死这个生意、直接加了上传 PDF 的功能之前。所以同样的事情，你知道的，你看到那样的小公司造着那些快 chatbot，赚一票快钱。但我们当时说，好吧，它们绝无可能在长期和有 VC 投资的初创公司竞争。这是不可能发生的，然后你同时看到，我们这么做的同时，美国有更大的公司处于隐身模式，对吧？那些 Sierra、Decagon 等等。但那是我们一开始看到的。我们现在看到的，是你说的后半部分：这个领域其实没那么拥挤。真正能把产品部署在受监管行业公司的本地环境里、并且具备它们在同等合规和安全水平下会要求的那种能力的玩家，还要能满足它们的 SLA 和数据要求。这样的玩家并不多，好吧。我们反复看到的都是同样几家。不是十七家玩家，不是的。好吧，你一只手就数得过来，而且那些横向的通用型玩家，我们也没那么常见到，对吧？所以当你把自己垂直化，或者不管你做什么，对吧？但当你选定一个特定框格去打的时候，我们感觉在这个领域里，我们没看到多少对手。现在，如果我们继续往下说，我们其实在进入金融服务之前就开始了。我们 2023 年造产品时，开始卖给电商，而在电商领域。显然我们看到了更多玩家，但也有更小的玩家。不过同样，还是那几个名字反复出现，我知道你有 Peter Thiel 那篇《竞争是失败者的事》，等等。再说一遍，我算什么，轮得到我说不同意见吗？但我会说，我不认为在我们这个阶段，杀死创业公司的是竞争，对吧？竞争会让你做愚蠢的事，比如抄袭其他玩家，或者朝第二个不同的方向走。说，哦，那帮人在那儿成了，我们去那儿。哦，他们在做这个。所以那一定是好的。可是不，那帮人和你一模一样。他们根本不知道自己在干什么。这个领域里的每个人在这个阶段都不知道自己在干什么。所以竞争让你做愚蠢的事，不是因为它逼你，而只是因为那是我们的天性使然。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: I mean, I find it's almost guaranteed that you're either going to have to fight status quo and people just not wanting to change or move. Because they don't really have a burning need, or you're going to have to find competitive vendors. The odds of you being in a place where everybody wants to buy and you're the only one selling. I mean, you know, if you're there, that's awesome. But, I just don't know how you could manufacture that situation.
zh: 我是说，我发现这几乎是注定的：你要么得对抗现状，对抗那些就是不想改变、不想动的人。因为他们并没有迫切的需要，要么你就得面对竞争性的供应商。你处在一个所有人都想买、而你是唯一一个在卖的境地的几率。我是说，你知道的，如果你在那儿，那太棒了。但是，我就是不知道你怎么能人为制造出那种局面。

speaker: Rafael Broshi
en: Me too. If you're going for an area where there's a gaping demand right now and the demand is growing by 100x a year. There's going to be competition there. There was competition in the dot com era. There's competition now, there's going to be competition in the future and if you look at the dot com era versus now, information flow is so different than it was, right? You can't compare what you're seeing now in terms of competition, but you also cannot compare the level of exposure you can get as a startup as well, right? I can reach any company I want anywhere in the world pretty easily. I'm not saying I'll be able to sell to them, but everything is much easier now. So it's like everything works together, more competition, more market opens up, the market grows faster. But I agree, it's all the same. It's like human nature. The easiest thing is to build something that is so complicated and so amazing that you don't have to talk to any potential customer ever and just keep building it, right? That's what everyone would want. That's like the dream but unfortunately, that's.
zh: 我也一样。如果你冲着一个眼下需求大开的领域去，而且需求每年增长 100 倍。那里一定会有竞争。互联网时代有竞争。现在有竞争，未来也会有竞争，而如果你把互联网时代和现在对比，信息流动和当年完全不同了，对吧？你现在在竞争层面看到的，没法和过去比，但你作为一个初创公司能获得的曝光度水平，同样也没法和过去比，对吧？我可以相当容易地触达世界上任何一家我想触达的公司。我不是说我能把东西卖给他们，但现在一切都容易多了。所以就像一切都在协同起作用，竞争更多，市场打开更多，市场增长更快。但我同意，本质都是一样的。就像人性。最容易的事就是造一个如此复杂、如此惊艳的东西，以至于你永远不用和任何潜在客户说话，只管埋头造它，对吧？那是所有人都想要的。那就像一个梦，但不幸的是，那。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Not life, yeah, not really.
zh: 不是生活，对，还真不是。

speaker: Rafael Broshi
en: Yeah.
zh: 对。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: What I'm curious, just on the fundraising side. How much had you raised by 2023?
zh: 我好奇的是，就融资这一面。到 2023 年你们一共融了多少钱？

speaker: Rafael Broshi
en: That was seven million dollars.
zh: 那是 700 万美元。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Normally you raise, you do the crypto thing, and then you're probably running out of money. You need to raise again. What was your kind of situation?
zh: 一般的路径是，你做了加密那个事，然后你大概就快没钱了。你需要再融一轮。你当时是怎样的局面？

speaker: Rafael Broshi
en: Yeah, so when we decided to pivot, we had $2 million left. Fired almost everyone. We're left with one, two engineers. Built the product for a year and a half. We didn't hire anyone for a year. Then we got to a point that we're almost cash flow positive. We burned $10,000, $20,000 a month.
zh: 对，我们决定转型的时候，手里还剩 200 万美元。裁掉了几乎所有人。最后只剩一两名工程师。造了一年半的产品。我们一年没招任何人。然后我们到了一个几乎现金流为正的点。我们每月烧 1 万、2 万美元。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: This was when? Now, '20, late '24-ish.
zh: 这是什么时候？现在，2020，2024 年底左右。

speaker: Rafael Broshi
en: That was, yeah, end of 2024. Investors told us things were picking up and we had our first six figure contract. A few hundred thousand dollars and when you're four or five people team, and eating noodles all day. You don't burn a lot of money. It's possible to build a product without burning a lot of money. But then you get to a point where you say, OK, either I'm continuing like this bootstrapped. It's going to be slow and the market is exploding, or we're going to raise more. So then we raised an additional $7 million and then we started ramping up and then we simply, we raised the $30 million.
zh: 那是，对，2024 年底。投资人告诉我们形势在好转，我们有了第一份六位数的合同。几十万美元，而当你只是四五人的团队、整天吃泡面的时候。你烧不了多少钱。不烧很多钱把产品造出来是可能的。但然后你会到一个节点说，好吧，要么我继续这样自力更生。那会很慢，而市场正在爆发，要么我们去融更多。于是我们又融了 700 万美元，然后我们开始提速，然后我们就是，我们融了那 3000 万美元。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Did you find that that was any harder? One thing I do find with competition is, if you have a lot of competition, it might not affect the business. Your business might be growing really fast, but it does tend to affect fundraising, or at least I've seen it affect more fundraising. Because it's just such an easy. Frankly VCs are like finding reasons to say no because you need so many, you got to just filter quickly and so competition is an easy one, too competitive, too competitive. Did you find that was the case? Did you find it was a little bit harder to fundraise? At some point your numbers are so big, it just doesn't matter anymore. Clearly you're winning, but in that seed stage, you know.
zh: 你有没有觉得那（轮）更难了一些？关于竞争我发现的一点是，如果你竞争者很多，它可能不影响业务。你的业务可能增长很快，但它确实往往影响融资，或者至少我见过它更多影响融资。因为这实在太容易了。坦白说 VC 们就是在找说「不」的理由，因为你需要见太多人，你必须快速过滤，所以竞争是一个现成的理由，太卷了、太卷了。你有没有发现情况是这样？你有没有发现融资难了一些？到某个点你的数字大到它就不再重要了。显然你在赢，但在种子轮阶段，你知道的。

speaker: Rafael Broshi
en: Yeah, always when you're in the extremes, everything doesn't matter, right? If you want to raise an A and you have a billion dollars in ARR, and you're growing five hundred percent. It's fine, you don't need a story. You don't need to meet anyone. You're going to get money. If you have $0, you're not going to get money. If you're in the few million dollars, that I get. VC space is business on steroids. I tell it to my parents that have businesses. This is nowhere like building a business. Maybe it's like that in the future, right? But it's extremely different. The KPIs are different. Working with VCs is different, and at the end of the day, a VC that invests in you and the seed round. All they need to really think about is will there be an investor that leads the A round, right? And the A round for B, and the B for C. Obviously building a business, it's important, we all know that. But it's gambling, right? It's building and putting money in a direction, and building a team of fifty people. Where your business warrants a team of five people and when you get there, building a team of five hundred.
zh: 对，凡是处在极端状态时，一切都无所谓了，对吧？如果你想融 A 轮，而且你有 10 亿美元的 ARR，还在以百分之五百的速度增长。那就没问题，你不需要故事。你不需要见任何人。钱会来的。如果你是 0 美元，你融不到钱。如果你是在几百万美元的量级，这个我懂。VC 这个行当是打了兴奋剂的生意。我跟我自己开公司的父母这么讲。这和经营一门生意毫无相似之处。也许未来会像那样，对吧？但它极其不同。KPI 不一样。和 VC 打交道的方式不一样，而归根结底，一个在种子轮投了你的 VC。他们真正需要想清楚的只是：会不会有投资人领投 A 轮，对吧？而 A 轮的看 B 轮，B 轮看 C 轮。显然把生意做好很重要，我们都知道。但这像是赌博，对吧？就是朝一个方向投入钱和建设，建一支五十人的团队。而你的业务其实只配得上五个人，等到了那个阶段，再建五百人的团队。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Needs to be somebody else to get to the next stage, that's right.
zh: 需要有别人来带你到下一个阶段，没错。

speaker: Rafael Broshi
en: Exactly, this is just the way it is. So it's very reasonable for a VC to only want to back the number one in a category. No one wants to back number three, no one and I think in a competitive space. The story is extremely important, and the story is not enough to say AI for customer support. Because there are a lot of those, but then you're competing with all of the best players in the world and then you're seeing a player that has raised $500 million and you raised seven and you're competing. You're still competing because they said, well, they took over the market, and things like, well, this is a $200 billion market and they have $75 million of ARR. It's not really taking the market, but those things don't really help, right? You need to explain why you're going to be the number one or front runner in a specific box in the market and why. So I think that's the important part, and the more competitive your market is, the more you need to crystallize the story. And it's very easy to say, well, I don't want to do that just for investors, but it's not. Every time I see that and I say that, I say, well, look, if you cannot crystallize it for your investors, you won't be able to crystallize it for customers. And VCs are not necessarily forward indicators of the market, but they are some derivative of what your customers are seeing. Because if everyone wants to buy you, you're going to be number one. If you are saying you have an amazing product, but your growth rate is not good. It means that customers are not buying you and it means there's something wrong. So before starting Notch, I was two years at a hedge fund. All I did was analyze companies, and when you're at a hedge fund and you don't speak to the companies. Public companies that you invest in, at the end of the day, what do you look at? You look at growth rate and you look at market share. If I'm looking at a large company and I see their growth rate is above the market and they have pricing power. They raise their prices by five percent a year, I don't need to know much else in terms of what is their position in the market. They have a great product, people like them, they have pricing power, it means everything. The smaller the company is, the less signals you have, the stronger your story needs to be. So it's always a blend between KPIs and story, and the more competitive the market is, the more fine tuned your story needs to be on how you're going to win at something. That's what everyone wants to bet on.
zh: 没错，事情就是这样。所以一个 VC 只想押品类里的第一名，是非常合理的。没人想投第三名，没人，而且我认为在一个竞争激烈的领域里。故事极其重要，而故事不能只说一句 AI 客服。因为那样的公司一大堆，而且那样你就是在和全世界最顶级的玩家们正面竞争，然后你看到一个融了 5 亿美元的玩家，而你融了七百万，你们在竞争。你还在竞争，因为大家会说，嗯，他们已经拿下了市场，以及诸如此类的话，比如，好吧，这是个 2000 亿美元的市场，而他们只有 7500 万美元的 ARR。这真谈不上拿下市场，但那些话也没用，对吧？你需要解释为什么你会成为市场中某个特定框格里的第一名或领跑者，以及为什么。所以我认为那才是重要的部分，而且你的市场竞争越激烈，你就越需要把故事打磨得清晰。说「我不想只是为了投资人这么做」很容易，但不是这么回事。每次我看到或说到这一点，我都会说，听着，如果你不能为投资人把它讲清楚，你就无法为客户把它讲清楚。而且 VC 未必是市场的先行指标，但他们是你客户所見的某种衍生品。因为如果人人都想买你，你就会是第一名。如果你说你有一个惊艳的产品，但你的增长率不好。那就意味着客户没有在买你，就意味着哪里出了问题。所以在创办 Notch 之前，我在一家对冲基金干了两年。我做的全部事情就是分析公司，而当你在对冲基金、又不和你投资的那些公司说话的时候。上市公司，归根结底，你看什么？你看增长率，你看市场份额。如果我看一家大公司，我看到它的增长率高于市场，而且它有定价权。它每年提价百分之五，那关于它在市场中的地位，我不需要知道太多别的。它有一个很棒的产品，人们喜欢它，它有定价权，这意味了一切。公司越小，你得到的信号越少，你的故事就得越强。所以这永远是 KPI 和故事之间的混合，而市场竞争越激烈，你就越需要把「你将如何在一个事情上取胜」的故事调得越精细。那是所有人都想押注的东西。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Yeah, you need to find that kind of sweet spot between, because obviously if you narrow it too much, then you're like, oh, but then that's too small of a market. It's too niche. So you've got to find that sweet spot where the opportunity is still big. You could still create a five to ten billion dollar company. But you're clearly going all in in a certain direction, in a certain position that nobody else is really going all in on. That doesn't mean they don't compete. They compete there, but it's like, hey, they're actually spending seventy percent of their time doing this stuff and I'm spending a hundred percent of my time doing this thing. So we'll cross over, but frankly, we'll probably beat them most of the time in this place. Because we're all in on this place, you know, something like that.
zh: 对，你需要找到那种甜点位，因为显然如果你切得太窄，那别人就会说，哦，可那样市场就太小了。太细分了。所以你得找到那个甜点位：机会依然够大。你依然能造出一家 50 到 100 亿美元的公司。但你明显在朝某个方向、某个别人没有真正 all in 的位置上 all in。这不代表他们不在那里竞争。他们在那里竞争，但就像是，嘿，他们实际上把百分之七十的时间花在这类事情上，而我把百分之百的时间花在这件事上。所以我们会有交叉，但坦白说，在这个地盘我们大概率会经常赢他们。因为我们在这个地方是 all in，你知道的，诸如此类。

speaker: Rafael Broshi
en: And I also think about it a bit differently in the sense of, I do think that every time I go on a call with the VC. That VC probably wants me to be the best founder that they've ever met. I mean, that's their job. They want to invest. When I interview people, if I interview six people a day. I don't go in saying, oh, this guy, I'm sure he's not going to be good, right? The guy goes into my interview, all I want right now is for this person to blow me away. That's all I want. So that's what VCs want as well, right? They meet startups. They want to say, oh my God, this guy's the best founder with the best story I've ever met. This is the craziest company, is going to be worth trillions of dollars, right? You just have to give them a reason why this is the case and if you cannot give them a reason why this is the case, then you should not be surprised why they don't want to invest in you. That's all. Now, if you're a good enough grade, then you're not going to get money from Sequoia. You're going to get money from others. Maybe you are that good, but maybe right now you had a bad round. Maybe you were scaling the business, right? Maybe you did a lot of other things while other people grabbed the market. No one knows what's gonna happen in two years, right? Some companies struggle in their A, some companies struggle in their B, some companies struggle in their C. Most companies struggle somewhere, most companies, right? So it shouldn't bother you, right? You have to raise, otherwise you're gonna die. But if you're raising, you need to do, I would say, the minimum amount between perfecting the raise versus perfecting what you believe is the right strategy for the company. Hopefully those two align, but sometimes they don't completely.
zh: 而且我也用一种略微不同的方式想这件事，我的意思是，我确实认为每次我和 VC 开会。那个 VC 大概率希望我是他们见过的最好的创始人。我是说，那是他们的工作。他们想投资。当我面试人的时候，如果我一天面六个人。我不会进去就说，哦，这家伙，我确定他不会好，对吧？这个人走进我的面试间，我此刻想要的全部，就是这个人把我彻底震住。那就是我想要的全部。VC 们想要的也是一样，对吧？他们见创业公司。他们想说，天哪，这家伙是我见过的最好的创始人、带着最好的故事。这是最疯狂的公司，会值几万亿美元，对吧？你只需要给他们

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: So let's spend the last few minutes just going very tactical. You've been selling to Enterprise for a few years now and I mean, nothing is easy. But I think especially when it's a small startup selling to a large enterprise, there's always something about that that is especially hard. Tell me a little bit, maybe some lessons learned, some tactics that founders can really use when they're selling enterprise. Maybe let's start at the top. The first part being you've got to get in the room. I mean, you've got to actually get somebody to listen to you, to hear you. Which you can't do through Google AdWords or Facebook ads or the sort of things that might work in SMB or mid market. How do you get the right people in the room to begin with?
zh: 那么让我们用最后几分钟来聊一些非常实操的东西。你卖企业客户已经有几年了,我是说,没有什么事是容易的。但我觉得尤其是当一家小初创公司卖给一家大企业时,总有一些东西是特别难的。跟我讲讲,也许是一些经验教训、一些创始人卖企业客户时真正能用得上的战术。也许让我们从最上面说起。第一部分是你得进到房间里。我是说,你得真正让某个人听你说话、听见你。这是你没法通过 Google AdWords 或 Facebook 广告、或者那些在 SMB 或中型市场可能管用的东西做到的。一开始你怎么让合适的人进到房间里?

speaker: Rafael Broshi
en: First of all, there is no formula for that. At the end of the day, it's all about connection and relationship. And the higher up you manage to build a relationship with, the better this is going to be. Now, you cannot just work the CEO. The CEO of a larger company, he might be the decision maker. He might weigh things your way, but he's not gonna get you to the POC if you don't do a good job with innovation. OK, so you have to work both ways, bottom up and up down. And up down, that's using all of your relations. Just hustle, hustle, hustle, hustle. That's all it is. Use all of your investors, use all of your employees, use your father, use your mother, use your brothers, use your sisters, use everyone you know. Everyone wants to help you. Everyone wants to help. If you're gonna ask help, everyone's gonna say yes. I really, I've never had anyone say no to me. I had people say, well, I don't know this guy. I'm not sure, maybe you can speak to this guy. Just ask, if you don't know him, who do you know, is there anyone else that can help me? A lot of people think that they need to come in a superior place asking for help and not really saying, hey, I really need your help, right? I need to close a sale there and I'm really looking for some from the company. Can you help me? It's much more sincere and people wanna see this kind of vulnerability. Everyone has it, I think, and again, I'm trying to be there. But I think the best founders that I see out there are those ones that, they don't care to put themselves out there. So that's one, in terms of coming from below. If you start talking to someone in the working level or talks with you in the first calls and you throw out too much that you came in through the CEO. This will not end well for you. You have to respect every person you talk to and you have to give them what they want and not what you have. It is fine to say, I don't have this, but listen to them and it's extremely hard, right? You want to sell what you have, but it is not how people buy. OK, and usually you might say, and I see this a lot where you say, well, but I'm talking to a company. An enterprise, and they don't have a pain point. I said, OK, great. If they don't have a pain point, you have nothing to sell. It doesn't matter what you're going to give them. It's fine, so just use the conversation to ask questions. What do they care about? They care about something. If you go on a call and a person say, well, yeah, I don't care about anything, right? I'm just here to pass the time. By the way, it does happen. It does happen, rarely, but it does happen that. Well, it's fine, you know, talk to him about life. But I think that's the key thing. Second, something that we didn't do as well when we started is thinking that in order to get an enterprise contract, you must slowly move up the ladder. I think there is zero connection between getting an enterprise deal and going from $10K to $50K to $100K to $200K, OK. It's just the fact that it's a rule of numbers, out of a hundred enterprises you're going to talk to, only probably five to ten of them will even consider working with a startup. So that's one. OK, ninety put aside, not relevant. Out of the five to ten, five might say, well, you know, I want more logos. They wouldn't care what and some might say, you know, that's fine. You know, one, you just need one. So I'm not saying don't try. Obviously, it's much easier when you have twenty logos. But it also happened to me where I had a lot of logos and the person said, well, you know, you don't have a company that does exactly this at that size, so it's not relevant. I'm like, so you want me to find the same company in a parallel universe? And then you figure out the real problems. Usually when you hear no, it's not just that you don't have specific clients. It's that something didn't add up. It's like when people tell you, hey, when an investor, when a VC says, no, I don't want to invest, right? Just take the no. Sometimes the response is not that accurate. Because why would they tell you, hey, I would never invest in you. I didn't like you, right? Never, it's either too early and it makes total sense when you think about it. So the same thing here, right? When people, when enterprise tells you, hey, you need more logos, the reason is probably different. OK, now the more logos you have, the easier it is because you have credibility. So they'll start by thinking that you probably have something to offer them. But if you don't, it's just about really pinpointing the pain point, OK. If someone can solve the exact thing you're looking for, usually you wouldn't care. At least not in meeting number one, meeting number two. Maybe you're going to fail security, right? That's fine, but you're going to get through those meetings. So I would say try to be extremely skeptic in what you sell and try to be very sharp in how you debrief what happened on the call in terms of, did I hit their pain point? And if not, why? Person didn't want to tell me, the pitch was off, my positioning sucks. It's usually that people always escape to my product's not good, the company doesn't care, they want us to have more logos. But it's not that most of the time. So I think all of the tips revolve around those points.
zh: 首先,对此没有公式。归根结底,这全是关于连接和关系。而你能建立起关系的人层级越高,事情就会越好。现在,你不能只搞定 CEO。大公司的 CEO,他可能是决策者。他可能会按你的方向来权衡事情,但如果你在创新方面做得不好,他不会把你引到 POC。好,所以你必须双向工作,自下而上和自上而下。而自上而下,那就是动用你所有的关系。就是拼命干,拼命干,拼命干,拼命干。就是这样而已。用上你所有的投资人,用上你所有的员工,用上你的父亲,用上你的母亲,用上你的兄弟,用上你的姐妹,用上你认识的每一个人。每个人都想帮你。每个人都想帮忙。如果你去请求帮助,每个人都会说好。我真的,从来没有人对我说不。我有人说过,嗯,我不认识这个人。我不确定,也许你可以跟那个人谈谈。就去问,如果你不认识他,你认识谁,还有没有其他人能帮我?很多人认为他们需要以一种高高在上的姿态来请求帮助,而不是真正说,嘿,我真的需要你的帮助,对吧?我需要在那里达成一笔交易,我真的很想从那家公司找一些人。你能帮我吗?这样更真诚,而且人们想看到这种脆弱。每个人都有,我觉得,而且再说一次,我在努力做到。但我觉得我在外面看到的最好的创始人是那些不在乎把自己暴露出来的人。所以这是一点,从自下而上的角度来说。如果你开始和某个基层层级的人交谈,或者在最初几通电话里和你谈的人,而你过多地抛出你是通过 CEO 进来的这件事。这对你不会有好结果。你必须尊重每一个你交谈的人,你必须给他们想要的东西,而不是你有的东西。说「我没有这个」是可以的,但要倾听他们,而这极其难,对吧

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: The no's are kind of easy in the sense that someone's like, I'm not interested. No pain point, OK, move on, right? And then the yes's are great. But there's these middle ones where it's like, yeah, we've been talking to them. They're interested. Maybe we even did either a proof of concept or an actual pilot. You did something, you signed some sort of initial MOU, like something, right? And it's just, but it's not getting you there. You're not getting to that final contract. Sometimes it's just, that's what it is. It takes six months, it takes twelve months and sometimes you're just wasting your time. How can you tease those two apart?
zh: 拒绝的情况其实比较容易处理,意思是有人说,我不感兴趣。没有痛点,好,继续往下走,对吧?然后同意的情况很棒。但还有那些中间地带的情况,就像,嗯,我们一直在跟他们谈。他们有兴趣。也许我们甚至做了概念验证或者一个实际的试点。你做了点什么,你签了某种初步的 MOU,诸如此类的东西,对吧?但它就是没能让你到达那里。你没能拿到那份最终合同。有时候就是这样,事情就是这样。它需要六个月,需要十二个月,有时候你就是在浪费时间。你怎么能把这两种情况区分开?

speaker: Rafael Broshi
en: So usually, and it happened to us as well, working with an enterprise. If they're going to spend the time to do an actual POC with you, things will probably move. OK, it's not something that someone can decide. What could happen is that you're doing a POC with them, which they did not consider a POC. As an example, you might speak to someone who is not the business owner. Well, there's someone from the tech department in a company, and you're pitching, and you're pitching. We have a great platform for document ingestion and an AI agent, and this and that. And you excite the guy, the guy, the woman, they're from the tech team. They want to see capabilities and they're like, well I can show you this and that. And yeah sure I'd love to see, and they're like, well if you get me a document I can do this. This happened to us about a year ago. I was so excited. It's like, yeah, I'm going to get you documents, right? And you're getting documents and you're like, we're in a POC with a five thousand people company. Then you finish the POC. Great, look, we don't see any need right now, or we're going to be in. Because it wasn't a POC, a real POC and again, it's everything that the books say. We're all wrong about that. We all made those mistakes because you have wishful thinking. You want to go into POCs, but POCs should be budgeted. You should take money for them. You should meet the business owner. You should understand the use case. You should also not be afraid to ask questions. Hey, what are the KPIs for the POC? What happens if we succeed? How's the process going forward? How would that look like? If people want your product and you send an offer. They're not going to move out just because you wrote a number they don't like. OK, If they want to do a POC with you and you say it's a $50,000 POC, and they want to do a POC with you but they think it's an outrageous price. They're going to tell you this is an outrageous price. They're going to do something about it. But companies, I feel especially in the US. They understand that if they want a good partner and a vendor. They need to pay, they need to put in the resources. OK, so I really feel that they're very fair as long as you do the process correctly. So usually in those kinds of deals that get stuck, it's because if you really go back and ask, did I meet the relevant people? Did I ask the relevant questions? Was it really a full blown POC or did I spend seventy thousand man hours in my company to prepare a POC that someone looked at once? It's not a real POC, so I think those are the cases. If it's just stuck, yeah, that's the risk in enterprise, right? Someone changes jobs, your champion leaves. You have to build as many intricate connections at the same time in a company. Don't stop meeting people. Don't stop trying to build connections in every level. That's the only way to make those kind of projects work.
zh: 通常来说,跟我们合作企业时也发生过这种情况——如果他们愿意花时间跟你做一个真正的 POC,事情很可能会有进展。好,这不是某个人就能决定的事情。可能发生的情况是,你在跟他们做一个 POC,而他们并没有把这当作一个 POC。举个例子,你可能跟一个不是业务负责人的人交谈。嗯,公司技术部门里有个人,你在推销,你在推销。我们有一个很棒的文档摄取平台和一个 AI 智能体,还有这个那个。然后你让这家伙兴奋了,这家伙,这个女的,他们来自技术团队。他们想看看能力,然后他们说,嗯,我可以给你展示这个和那个。然后好啊当然我想看看,然后他们说,嗯,如果你给我一份文档,我可以做这个。这件事大概一年前发生在我们身上。我当时非常兴奋。就像是,对,我会给你弄到文档的,对吧?然后你拿到了文档,然后你觉得,我们正在跟一家五千人的公司做 POC。然后你做完了 POC。很好,你看,我们现在看不出任何需求,或者我们将会加入。因为那不是一个 POC,一个真正的 POC,而且再说一次,这就是书上说的那些东西。我们在这件事上都错了。我们都犯过那些错误,因为你抱有一厢情愿的想法。你想进入 POC,但 POC 应该有预算。你应该为它们拿到钱。你应该见业务负责人。你应该理解用例。你也不应该害怕问问题。嘿,这个 POC 的 KPI 是什么?如果我们成功了会怎样?后续流程是怎么样的?那会是什么样子?如果人们想要你的产品,而你发了一份报价。他们不会仅仅因为你写了一个他们不喜欢的数字就退出。好,如果他们想跟你做 POC,你说这是一个五万美元的 POC,他们想跟你做 POC 但他们觉得这是个离谱的价格。他们会告诉你这是个离谱的价格。他们会为此做点什么。但是公司们,我觉得尤其是美国的。他们明白,如果他们想要一个好的合作伙伴和供应商。他们需要付钱,他们需要投入资源。好,所以我真的觉得,只要你把流程做对,他们是非常公平的。所以通常在那类卡住的交易里,是因为如果你真的回头去问,我见到相关的人了吗?我问了相关的问题了吗?那真的是一个完整的 POC,还是我在自己公司里花了七万个人时去准备一个某人只看了一次的 POC?那不是一个真正的 POC,所以我认为那些就是这类情况。如果就是卡住了,是的,这就是企业级销售的风险,对吧?有人换了工作,你的支持者离开了。你必须同时在一家公司里建立尽可能多的深层联系。不要停止见人。不要停止在每个层级建立联系。那是让这类项目运转起来的唯一办法。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Perfect, last question, we'll end on this. What would be a top piece of advice that you find yourself giving pretty often to early stage founders?
zh: 很好,最后一个问题,我们就以这个结束。你发现自己经常给早期创始人的一条最重要建议是什么?

speaker: Rafael Broshi
en: I'd say I ask, who are your dream customers? And they give me a list or something. I said, OK, go talk to them. Well, we don't have a product. We don't have this. We don't have that. We're not sure. We don't have any other. No, that's the wrong way to go. Don't go the long route. Talk to your dream customers first. Just go to them. Because those are the people you're after, right? And if they're not interested, at least you know it now. But people are afraid and I was as well. That's a mistake I made.
